sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Compared to traditional separate energy systems, integrated energy systems consider
the production, transmission, conversion, and consumption of different energy forms (elec-
tricity, heat, gas, cooling, etc.) in a unified manner, offering significant advantages such as
higher flexibility and better complementarity. As an integral mechanism for energy conser-
vation, emission reduction, and improved energy utilization efficiency, integrated energy
systems provide robust support for achieving the “Dual Carbon” goals [ 1,2]. In [ 3], the
stepped carbon trading cost is incorporated within the carbon emission framework, with
case studies demonstrating that the stepped carbon trading mechanism further reduces
Electronics 2026, 15, 933 https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15050933
Electronics 2026, 15, 933 2 of 25
carbon emissions compared to the traditional Carbon Emissions Trading (CET) mecha-
nism. In [4], Fan examines how carbon quota and trading policies affect carbon emissions,
demonstrating that appropriately calibrated institutional coefficients in the carbon trading
mechanism can lead to a win–win outcome for both economic efficiency and low-carbon
sustainability. In [5], an integrated scheduling model combining green certificate trading
(GCT) and carbon trading is proposed. The inherent synergy and convertibility between
these two mechanisms drive higher renewable energy accommodation and lower carbon
emissions. Li [6] established a low-carbon scheduling model for IES incorporating wind
power, PV , and hydrogen storage. By introducing P2G technology and carbon capture
equipment to achieve multi-energy coupling, the model effectively enhances the accom-
modation of wind and PV power while promoting deep decarbonization of the system.
Yang [7] proposed an optimization scheduling model for low-carbon community IES con-
sidering resource flexibility and segmented control of solid oxide fuel cells. The proposed
method effectively promoted low-carbon economic operation of the system by mobilizing
different types of energy storage equipment and load-side flexible resources. A novel
modular distributed framework, introduced in [8], serves as a key solution for unlocking
greater flexibility and enhanced profitability in nuclear-renewable hybrid energy systems.
However, as the proportion of renewable energy increases, its output uncertainty
amplifies the difficulty of system regulation [ 9]. Concurrently, fluctuations on the load
side increase supply–demand uncertainty. This presents a substantial challenge to the
secure and stable operation of IES, thereby necessitating enhanced flexible regulation
capacities. In [10], IES flexibility is defined as the system’s ability to regulate energy supply,
demand, and power flows effectively within a designated area while ensuring stable
operation. Flexibility resources are the prerequisite for system flexibility. In [11], flexibility
resources are defined as adjustable generating units, energy storage devices, responsive
flexible loads, electric vehicles, and other resources within the power system. Demand
response, as a critical measure for regulating load power and promoting supply–demand
balance, additionally plays a significant role in enhancing system flexibility [12]. In [13], a
multi-objective optimization model simultaneously considering electricity and gas demand
response is established. The objective functions include the economic cost of the IES
and user satisfaction, effectively reducing end-user load fluctuations and enhancing load-
shifting efficiency. In [14], the enhancement effect of multiple flexibility resources on overall
system flexibility is analyzed; fully leveraging and integrating diverse flexibility resources
boosts wind power accommodation and reduces carbon emissions. To address system
flexibility demands, reference [15] quantifies demands via segmented renewable outputs.
Similarly, a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning-based strategy for distributed energy
hubs is proposed to enable safe scheduling under carbon trading costs while protecting
sensitive data through differential privacy. This approach enhances operational flexibility
by coordinating hydrogen, gas, and storage resources in a decentralized manner [ 16].
In [17], a low-carbon economic scheduling framework for multi-microgrids is introduced.
By minimizing both operating cost and carbon emissions, this work demonstrated the
potential of advanced learning-based strategies to improve flexibility and sustainability.
Arvanitidis [18] focused on a novel nuclear integrated energy system configuration that
combines small modular reactors, renewable energy sources, energy storage, and a thermal
network coupled with the IEEE-30 Bus system for security-constrained economic dispatch.
By integrating nuclear base load generation with intermittent RES, the approach enhanced
operational flexibility and efficiency in complex energy configurations.
Electric vehicles (EVs) serve as flexibility resources, offering new possibilities for
optimizing demand response and electricity markets. In [ 19], a two-stage optimization
strategy for EV charging and discharging based on the PSO algorithm is proposed. This
https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15050933
Electronics 2026, 15, 933 3 of 25
strategy comprehensively considers EV charging demands and grid operational conditions,
optimizing EV charging behavior through demand response mechanisms. It enhances grid
stability and improves economic benefits for EV users. In [20], the flexibility of large-scale
electric buses is quantified, effectively evaluating both their upward and downward flexi-
bility. Additionally, it demonstrates the potential for fleet operators to generate additional
economic revenue by providing such flexibility to the flexibility market.
An integrated energy system is a comprehensive platform that spans energy pro-
duction, transmission, and consumption, involving multiple stakeholders such as system
operators and end-users. In [ 21], power grids and gas networks are treated as distinct
entities, with game-theoretic interactions between them fully considered to balance their
interests. In [ 22], a Stackelberg game-based IES scheduling optimization framework is
established to reconcile interests between IES operators and users, effectively coordinating
their relationship. A non-cooperative game and multi-energy pricing strategy is employed
in [23] for IES demand-side management. The results demonstrate successful coordi-
nated optimization between users and suppliers, leading to reduced peak–valley load
ratios and lower energy costs. In [ 24], a virtual power plant optimization configuration
method considering multi-entity participation of electric vehicles and load aggregators
is proposed; through this coordinated mechanism, enhanced operational sustainability
with improved power supply reliability, reduced charging disorderliness, and low-carbon
economic operation is achieved.
To solve the scheduling model, various methods have been employed. In [25], an IES
optimization operation model incorporating stochastic robust optimization for electric vehi-
cles and the participation of user aggregators is established. By considering the uncertainty
of EV charging behaviors and user demand response, this model optimizes the economic
operation of IES, reduces economic losses for users, and lowers the system’s total opera-
tional costs. In [ 26], a bi-level game dispatch model is proposed for the park integrated
energy system (PIES), where the synergy of electricity-carbon market decision-making is
explicitly considered. The improved alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)
is used to solve the distributed optimization problem. Liu [27] constructs a hybrid game
architecture with the energy system operator as the main body and the RIES alliance as
the slave, and the hybrid game process is solved using Genetic Algorithm. The Particle

sections.title: 2.1 Flexibility Demand Situation
sections.text:
The flexibility demand of IES mainly originates from the volatility and uncertainty
of wind energy, solar energy, and load. In addition, the anti-peak shaving characteristics
of wind and solar power output may cause the net load curve to fluctuate in the opposite
trend to the load curve.
The relationship between net load and flexibility resource output usually falls into
three scenarios: When the net load fluctuation exceeds the upper limit of flexibility resource
output, the system cannot meet the upward flexibility demand, which may lead to energy
supply interruption or unstable system operation. When the net load remains between
the upper and lower limits of flexibility resource output, the system can better meet the
flexibility demand and achieve supply–demand balance. When the net load fluctuation is
lower than the lower limit of flexibility resource output, the system faces the inability to
meet the downward flexibility demand, resulting in resource surplus, which may cause
waste of idle resources and economic losses.
According to the directional characteristics of flexibility, the upward and downward
flexibility demands of IES can be expressed by the following equations:

sections.title: 2.2 Flexibility Supply Situation
sections.text:
Flexibility resources on the source and energy storage sides have the characteristics
of convenient control and flexible scheduling. As a special flexibility resource, demand
response on the load side provides new ideas and strategies for IES. This demand re-
sponse mechanism improves the operation efficiency and flexibility of the entire IES by
incentivizing users to adjust their power consumption behavior.

sections.title: 3 Dispatch Model for IES Considering Flexibility and
sections.text:
Multi-Entity Participation
Against the backdrop of steady power market reforms, a new competitive landscape
has evolved, marked by the participation of multiple entities such as IES operators and
competition among diverse market elements. This paper develops a bi-layer optimal
dispatch model featuring multi-entity participation. The upper layer optimizes IES operator
revenue and system flexibility while incorporating the GCT-CET mechanism; the lower
layer accounts for user aggregator costs and the individual benefits of EVs. As the upper-
layer leader, the IES operator can give priority to releasing price strategies for electric energy,
thermal energy, and cooling energy; user aggregators and electric vehicles, as lower-layer
participants, can implement more reasonable demand response strategies and charging–
discharging plans according to changes in energy prices to ensure the optimization of their
own goals, and at the same time, promptly feed back their own energy usage adjustments
to the IES operator. The two-layer optimization model is shown in Figure 1, and the IES
structure diagram is shown in Figure 2.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Constraints
sections.text:
In the IES, various supply–demand relationships such as electric energy and thermal
energy are mutually constrained, and its operation is restricted by various constraints.
These constraints include electric power balance constraints, cold and heat power balance
constraints, as well as equipment output and ramping constraints. These constraints jointly
act on the operating state of the IES, ensuring that the system maintains stable and efficient
overall operation while meeting various load demands.

sections.title: 3.3 Formatting of Mathematical Components
sections.text:
The optimized dispatch model considering multi-entity participation proposed in this
paper is a two-layer optimization model. Compared with the single-level model, both the
upper and lower layer of the model have their own objective functions, constraints, and
independent decision variable outputs. In this model, the charging/discharging power
and state of charge of electric vehicles, as well as the purchased energy of user aggregators
from the lower-layer model, are transmitted as decision variables to the upper-layer model
to re-solve the upper-layer objective. Through the mutual iteration between the upper and
lower layers, the global optimal solution of the two-layer model is finally obtained.
To reduce the probability of particles falling into local optimal, the PSO algorithm
with improved parameters by the Dung Beetle Optimizer (DBO) is selected to solve the
upper-layer model, while the lower-layer model is solved using CPLEX 12.10 software.
The solution obtained by the improved PSO algorithm is not unique but forms a Pareto
front. In this paper, the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS)
is used to select a compromise solution from the Pareto front for subsequent analysis [24].
To select a final compromise dispatch scheme from the Pareto optimal solution set,
this study use the objective function values (i.e., the operating profit of the IES operator and

sections.title: 3.3.2 The Solution Procedure
sections.text:
The solution procedure of this paper is as follows:
1. Input typical daily electric, thermal, and cooling load data, as well as wind and solar
power output data, and relevant device parameters.
2. Initialize the improved PSO algorithm, randomly generate relevant variables, and set
the population size and maximum number of iterations.
3. Solve the lower-level model using CPLEX 12.10 software to obtain the optimal values
and transmit variables such as purchased energy to the upper-level model.
4. Calculate the upper-level objective function values and record the individual best and
global best solutions.
5. Check if the maximum number of iterations is reached. If not, update the velocity and
position of each particle according to the improved PSO algorithm, and transmit relevant
energy price variables to the lower-level model. If yes, output the Pareto front solution set.
